title: The tools we built while making a 4-player co-op pixel-art RPG with AI coding agents
author: Cr3L4real
selftext:
I'm building **Neon Kabuki 2089**, a browser-based top-down co-op action RPG set in Kabukichō in 2089 ( [neonkabuki.com](http://neonkabuki.com) ). AI agents (Claude Code) write nearly all the code. The most useful work turned out to be the tools we built around the game:

* **God Hand (World Studio + Asset Studio).** These are standalone editors for dressing one area of the city with palette-locked pixel props like vending machines, manholes and signs. Placement rules are built in: upright props hug walls, nothing stands mid-sidewalk, and only flat props can go on roads. Each scene has a prop budget. Every time, it's rebuilt fresh from the latest code so it never shows an outdated map.
* **Headless screenshot tool.** One command opens the game, jumps to any spot and saves a screenshot. Every visual change needs one, and the agent has to actually look at it instead of assuming it rendered.
* **Map art preview.** Renders any rectangle of the map to an image. After a map change we diff it against a "before" image to prove the original district wasn't touched.
* **Lag simulator + bot clients.** Browser tests run 4 players under 0/80/150 ms of lag plus jitter, and scripted test clients drive the server in protocol tests.
* **Review flags.** New effects (hacking, weapon, boss FX) ship behind URL flags like `?hackfx=1`, so I can review them in the live game before anyone else sees them.
* **Local admin dashboard.** Shows who played and for how long, plus bug reports and browser errors from playtesters. It's visible only on my PC and stores no addresses.

**Workflow and art consistency:** Every agent reads one shared rules file with the project's invariants, decisions (with reasons) and known gotchas. Each session ends by updating a checkpoint file, so nothing depends on chat memory. For art, everything follows one style guide mirrored in a theme file: six palette colors plus three state colors, and code may not add new color literals. The pixel art is drawn in code rather than generated images, and any new look starts as one test scene that I approve in a playtest before it rolls out city-wide.

What tools have you built around your AI workflow?

replies.author: Cr3L4real
replies.body: I mix some in the video to give a better perspective. In the game you have 3 zoom levels you can switch between depending on your playstyle. Did you play the game?

replies.author: irateas
replies.body: I just see the gameplay and - assets are inconsistent. Sorry - but cars aren't aligned with perspective. This is an issue. I would understand if you said - "work in progress - will fix this". No I haven't played it. But can just look at the videos and see the issue. Not saying that to hate on the game - just bring helpful feedback. I am tired of lazy implementations in AI based games. If that's in progress I get it. But if is not - lazy. Hope this helps

replies.author: Cr3L4real
replies.body: This is a work in progress and that isn't something I had considered. The entire point of any of my post is about getting helpful feedback. I would call this a prototype or alpha at best. I had stopped expanding it last week and started trying to polish and make it more coherent. A couple days ago I couldn't help but to start to add another area, but wanted more feedback before I did. Thanks for your feedback!!

replies.author: irateas
replies.body: No worries. Hope this feedback will help 🤞
